briefs.16e874d58dd170be: The question asks whether the first published seasonally adjusted initial claims figure for the week ending 2026-11-21 is strictly above 203,000; exactly 203,000 is not above. The DOL release of 2026-11-19 gave an advance 203,000 for the week ending 2026-11-14, up 1,000 from a revised 202,000 for the prior week (https://www.dol.gov/ui/data.pdf, 2026-11-19). The week ending 2026-11-07 was first printed at 200,000 against a 195,000 consensus (https://www.verifiedinvesting.com/blogs/us-economic-metrics/jobless-claims-week-ending-november-7-2026, 2026-11-12) and later revised up to 202,000, and the week ending 2026-10-31 stands at 191,000. The 4-week average is 197,750, and only two of the last twelve revised weeks (207,000 each, late Aug and early Sep) exceed 203,000. The target release is Wednesday 2026-11-25 at 8:30 a.m. ET because of Thanksgiving (https://www.financecalendar.com/event/us-initial-jobless-claims-november-25-2026/), and no consensus had been published as of 2026-11-20. In the revised FRED series, about 82% of weeks since 2025 and 63% of weeks in 2026 were above 203,000 (https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/fredgraph.csv?id=ICSA), but that is a revised series and the recent level sits right at the threshold, so the long-run share overstates the odds. A year ago the pre-Thanksgiving week printed 216,000, down 6,000 from the prior week, and Bloomberg notes holiday-week swings (https://www.ttnews.com/articles/jobless-claims-nov-22-2025, 2025-11-26). Recent first prints have tended to be revised up afterward, which does not count for resolution but suggests first prints run slightly low. Unadjusted claims were 197,492 for the week ending 2026-11-14 against 218,228 a year earlier, so the level is lower than last year. The answer would move up if the consensus forms above 205,000 or if other labor data show layoffs rising, and down if consensus sits near 198,000 or lower.
